“And Abraham was ninety years old and nine, when he was circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin.” “And Ishmael his son was thirteen years old, when he was circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin.”

Abraham was not circumcised on the eighth day after he was born; he was ninety-nine. Ishmael was thirteen. There was no eighth day, no days of purifying and no sacrifice. That is circumcision of the fathers, not circumcision after the manner of Moses.

The Pharisees wanted circumcision and sacrifice together, after the manner of Moses, because sacrificing was their bread and butter. As more people followed Christ, more of them stopped sacrificing, and if the people stop sacrificing, the Pharisees cannot eat. So they went into the churches saying you have to be circumcised to be saved. That is not what the Bible, Christ or the apostles taught. They were trying to put back on the people the yoke that could not be borne, the same one Peter asked about: “why tempt ye God, to put a yoke upon the neck of the disciples, which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear?”

“And the Lord visited Sarah as he had said”, and “Sarah conceived, and bare Abraham a son in his old age, at the set time of which God had spoken to him.” Sarah conceived in old age and Abraham named the child Isaac. Then: “And Abraham circumcised his son Isaac being eight days old, as God had commanded him.” “And Abraham was an hundred years old, when his son Isaac was born unto him.”

Isaac was circumcised on the eighth day, as God commanded, but this was long before Moses. There is no reading of them going and sacrificing animals for it. So even eighth-day circumcision here is not after the manner of Moses. There is circumcision of the fathers, and there is circumcision after the manner of Moses, which carries the sacrifice.

That is how Paul can say in Galatians 5, “if ye be circumcised, Christ shall profit you nothing.” He means circumcised after the manner of Moses, back under the yoke of bondage, taught by the Pharisees that you must be circumcised and sacrifice an animal to be saved. “For I testify again to every man that is circumcised, that he is a debtor to do the whole law.” Once the temple was destroyed and the priests scattered, that man had no way to keep it and was finished.

“Christ is become of no effect unto you, whosoever of you are justified by the law; ye are fallen from grace.” Christ's sacrifice does away with the animal sacrifice, so whoever runs back to animals to atone for sin rejects what Christ did on the cross. Paul is not throwing out the commandments. He is rejecting the sacrifice that was bewitching the Galatians. So “Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage.”

If circumcision after the manner of Moses is circumcision with sacrifice, is all circumcision of Moses? Christ answers it: “Moses therefore gave unto you circumcision; (not because it is of Moses, but of the fathers;) and ye on the sabbath day circumcise a man.”

Moses gave it to them, but circumcision is not of Moses. It is of the fathers, of Abraham, who was the one first circumcised. So when Acts 15 says circumcised after the manner of Moses, that is not the same thing as the circumcision of Abraham.

There are two different things here: circumcision of the fathers, and circumcision after the manner of Moses with the sacrifice of Leviticus 12 behind it. Seeing that difference is what opens up what the Pharisees were demanding and what Paul was fighting in his letters.

In Acts 15 certain men came down from Judea and taught, “Except ye be circumcised after the manner of Moses, ye cannot be saved.” Why does it say after the manner of Moses and not just circumcision? Leviticus 12 shows the manner of Moses. A woman who “conceived seed, and born a man child” is unclean seven days; “in the eighth day the flesh of his foreskin shall be circumcised”; she continues in the blood of her purifying thirty-three more days, forty in all for a boy and eighty for a girl. When the days are fulfilled she brings a lamb and a pigeon or turtledove for a burnt offering and a sin offering, and if she cannot afford a lamb, “two turtles, or two young pigeons”. The priest makes the atonement, and the offering covers the child as well as the mother.

Luke 2 confirms it with Mary and Christ. Mary conceived seed and bore a man child. “And when eight days were accomplished for the circumcising of the child, his name was called JESUS, which was so named of the angel before he was conceived in the womb.” That is the eighth day of Leviticus 12.

“And when the days of her purification according to the law of Moses were accomplished, they brought him to Jerusalem, to present him to the Lord”, because “Every male that openeth the womb shall be called holy to the Lord”. Then comes the offering: “to offer a sacrifice according to that which is said in the law of the Lord, A pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons.” Those are the offerings Leviticus 12:8 names.

So behind circumcision after the manner of Moses comes sacrifice. It is circumcision with the eighth day, the days of purifying and the offering for the woman and the child all tied together. That is what the men from Judea were pressing on the Gentiles, and that is why the scripture calls it the manner of Moses.

God told Isaac why the promise stood: “Because that Abraham obeyed my voice, and kept my charge, my commandments, my statutes, and my laws.” Abraham obeyed, and he kept the charge, the commandments, the statutes and the laws. That is past tense. It tells you what Abraham was doing from the beginning that proved his faith. His obedience was his acceptable faithfulness, the performance of Sirach 15:15.

Paul writes, “And the law is not of faith: but, The man that doeth them shall live in them.” The law meant there is the law of sacrifice, which came later. Abraham's faith came first, and his faith and the promise to him go hand in hand; the promise predates the law of sacrifice.

“Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us”. The curse of the law is condemnation, not being able to atone for every sin. Caiaphas pointed it out without knowing it: “it is expedient for us, that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation perish not.” Both the northern and southern kingdoms were under the old covenant they agreed to in Deuteronomy 27 and kept breaking, so both were condemned and destroyed by the nations. But the Lord loved them, sent his son to die for them, and took them out of that contract into a new one, “That the blessing of Abraham might come on the Gentiles through Jesus Christ”, meaning the northern kingdom.

Paul says “before faith came, we were kept under the law”, and “the law was our schoolmaster to bring us unto Christ, that we might be justified by faith.” The schoolmaster is the law of sacrifice, and the “we” is Israel. After faith came, “we are no longer under a schoolmaster.” Jews, Greeks, bond, free, male and female were all the same people of God in Christ.

“And if ye be Christ’s, then are ye Abraham’s seed, and heirs according to the promise.” Abraham is the father of faith, so his children should be children of faith like him: keeping the commandments the way he did, with faith in Christ instead of the animal sacrifice the Galatians were bewitched back into. The promise pertains to the Israelites, not to all nations.

Sirach 15:15 says, “If thou wilt, to keep the commandments, and to perform acceptable faithfulness.” Keeping God's commandments is performing acceptable faithfulness: those are your actions, and that is where your faith lies. Your works prove your faith and your faith proves your works; they go hand in hand. God “hath set fire and water before thee: stretch forth thy hand unto whether thou wilt.”

For anyone still confused, Sirach 19:20 says it again: “The fear of the Lord is all wisdom; and in all wisdom is the performance of the law, and the knowledge of his omnipotency.” The performance of the law is the acceptable faithfulness of Sirach 15. Wisdom is not only knowing the law; it is performing it.

The words “the knowledge of his omnipotency” mean knowing that God is all around us, and we acknowledge it by keeping his laws.

This is what Habakkuk and Paul mean by the just living by faith. Paul says “the law is holy, and the commandment holy, and just, and good.” The just are those who keep God's laws and commandments, and they live by faith in Christ. Fearing God, keeping his law and living by faith are one walk.

The “he” of Daniel 7:25 is the fourth kingdom Daniel did not understand, which the angel revealed to Ezra as the eagle with three heads: Rome, America and Britain. Daniel says “he shall speak great words against the most High”, blasphemies, “and shall wear out the saints of the most High”. Like a pair of sneakers worn so long you cannot tell what brand they were, slavery wore us out until nobody recognizes us as the Israelites, the glorious and mighty sons and daughters of God. People go, those are some damn black Africans. Now you look at a negro Latino and you go, I don't know what the hell that is. That thing, a negro, was made up, and nobody can identify them people as a race.

Then the part about time: he shall “think to change times and laws”. To see what he changed, go to what God set. “This month shall be unto you the beginning of months: it shall be the first month of the year to you.”

God himself appointed the first month of the year for Israel, at the time he brought them out of Egypt. The new year is not a date man picks. It is an ordinance of God, and it is one of the times the fourth beast thought to change.

Which month did God make the beginning of months? “This day came ye out in the month Abib.” Abib is the name of the first month of the ancient Hebrew calendar, generally corresponding to parts of March and April in the modern Gregorian calendar: the end of March into the beginning of April, the spring season.

The word comes from Hebrew and literally means ear of grain, young green ears, sprouting. It refers to the stage when barley is ripe but still soft, marking the start of the spring harvest. God's new year begins in spring, when the barley comes in.

So when you see Israelites celebrating Passover in the winter, they don't know what the hell they are talking about. The new year was changed from spring to the dead of winter. That is what God warns us about in Daniel 7:25: he shall “think to change times and laws”.

“And God said, Let there be lights in the firmament of the heaven to divide the day from the night; and let them be for signs, and for seasons, and for days, and years”. The lights in the heavens were set by God to mark the times.

“And God made two great lights; the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night: he made the stars also.” The greater light is the sun, and the lesser light is the moon. When Adam and Eve were created, the moon was what they call the full moon; that was the beginning. God made two great lights. It does not say the moon was dark with only a little bit of light.

What did the white man do? He said, count from when the moon is black, or, as some say, from when it has that one sliver of light. That is not biblical. In the Bible the moon was made full. It confuses a lot of people, and there are Israelites who base holy days on when you cannot see the moon. We did that at one time too, so we are not hating; we are enlightening.

These lights are also how God swears to keep Israel. Jeremiah 31 speaks of the Lord “which giveth the sun for a light by day, and the ordinances of the moon and of the stars for a light by night”, and says, “If those ordinances depart from before me, saith the Lord, then the seed of Israel also shall cease from being a nation before me for ever.” Nobody can get rid of the sun, the moon or the stars, so Israel remains his people.

“Jesus answered, Are there not twelve hours in the day? If any man walk in the day, he stumbleth not, because he seeth the light of this world.” Christ says there are twelve hours in the day.

What the white man has done is make something called daylight saving time, where they move time forward or backward. They play with times. Daniel said this man would “think to change times and laws”, and here is one more way he has done it: even the hours of the day are shifted at his word.

God set the day by his light; man changes the clock. That is one of the times the fourth kingdom has changed on the whole world.

“And he exerciseth all the power of the first beast before him, and causeth the earth and them which dwell therein to worship the first beast, whose deadly wound was healed.” The first beast was Rome. You may think nobody worships Rome today. Really?

Look at the days of the week. Sunday is the sun, Monday the moon, Tuesday Mars, Wednesday Mercury, Thursday Jupiter, Friday Venus and Saturday Saturn. Now the months: January is named after the Roman god Janus, with two faces looking to the future and the past. February comes from Februalia, a Roman festival of purification and atonement. March is Mars, the Roman god of war. April comes from aperire, to open, like flowers in spring. May is the goddess Maia, June is the goddess Juno. July was Quintilis, the fifth month, until Julius Caesar named it after his family, and August was Sextilis until the emperor Augustus named it after himself. That is not the spirit. Throw it out. Let it go.

That's the liberal for you: oh, we love you niggers, I mean black people. Jacob knew Esau's heart. That is why he sent the gifts ahead: he thought Esau might be coming to kill him.

Hebrews explains what was working in Esau: “Looking diligently lest any man fail of the grace of God; lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you, and thereby many be defiled”. Looking diligently means looking within yourself. The root of bitterness is a hidden sin under the ground that nobody sees, but over time it springs up and troubles you. It distorts your thoughts and your perception, so that things you once saw clearly, with eyes anointed with eye salve, are no longer pure to you.

“Lest there be any fornicator, or profane person, as Esau, who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright.” Profane means devoted to what is not sacred, secular rather than religious: Esau was a carnal man, a man of the field, whose religion is sin. Now all of a sudden he cares about the birthright, just as his children want to stand in our place claiming to be the Jews and the people of the book. You got the children of God and you got the children of the devil; there is no in between. You either got the godly mind or the Edomite mind. Confusion is Satan's playground. Satan loves us operating in confusion. That is why his children throw every kind of confusion into the media and everywhere they go, and why leaders of other nations have said they do not want that American media in their countries. They know every evil work hides behind that cloud of confusion.

“the sons of God saw the daughters of men” in Genesis 6 is about men, not spirits; God says “My spirit shall not always strive with man, for that he also is flesh.” Psalms 82:6 shows who these sons of God are and what God calls them: “I have said, Ye are gods; and all of you are children of the most High.”

We are gods, and we are children of the Most High. That is why the sons of God in Genesis 6 are called by that name: they carried that DNA, made in the image of God.

It is also why their sin was so serious. Back in Genesis 6:4, “There were giants in the earth in those days; and also after that, when the sons of God came in unto the daughters of men.” The sons of God, the children of the Most High, took wives of the other nations, which was forbidden. The children born to them “became mighty men which were of old, men of renown,” and “God saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually.” So the Most High brought destruction, and later we had to pay for what we did as the sons of God; he told Abraham his seed would be afflicted in a land not theirs for four hundred years.

At the bush God told Moses, “Draw not nigh hither: put off thy shoes from off thy feet, for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground.” The Most High expects humility, that we humble ourselves before him. Moses was a great man in Egypt, second to Pharaoh, raised in all the customs of Egypt, and God said, I don't want to hear all of that. The shoes were symbolic.

Ecclesiastes 5:1 is what the Most High requires: “Keep thy foot when thou goest to the house of God, and be more ready to hear, than to give the sacrifice of fools: for they consider not that they do evil.” A lot of times we come with pride and contention, acting like we know. You don't know a damn thing, because if you did, you would not have followed white Jesus.

Our brothers and sisters in the world do not consider that they are in evil, and a lot of times when they come into the sanctuaries it is the same thing: pride, contention, thinking they know much when they do not. Keep thy foot means keep your mouth shut when you enter the house of God and be ready to hear, the same thing he told Moses.

The same is required of us coming into this truth. All the Christian garbage we learned, leave it outside. Islam, garbage, leave it outside. Nuwaubianism, Afrocentric, black power: all garbage. We must reform our minds as Israelites and meditate in these scriptures.

Moses asked what name to give the children of Israel, and “God said unto Moses, I AM THAT I AM: and he said, Thus shalt thou say unto the children of Israel, I AM hath sent me unto you.” So who was speaking to Moses out of the bush? You should already know: Christ.

John 8:58 proves it: “Jesus said unto them, Verily, verily, I say unto you, Before Abraham was, I am.” Before Abraham was, I am. The same I AM who sent Moses to Pharaoh is Christ, speaking before Abraham ever lived. It was Christ who spoke directly to Moses.

That is why Moses could teach the gospel in the wilderness. Christ held him up on the mountain for a long season, forty days and forty nights, and showed him the secrets of the times, the beginning, the middle and the end. The God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob who came down to deliver us out of Egypt is the anointed.

Christ spoke to Abram, before his name was changed to Abraham: “Know of a surety that thy seed shall be a stranger in a land that is not theirs, and shall serve them; and they shall afflict them four hundred years.” That seed runs through Isaac, not through Abraham’s other children; Paul expounds that in Romans 9. The other nations are not God’s chosen people. And this first affliction is not America; it is ancient Egypt, where Jacob and the souls with him walked in.

So why did God bring that judgment on us? What did the sons of God do? They mixed with the daughters of men. Genesis 6: “the sons of God saw the daughters of men that they were fair; and they took them wives of all which they chose.” The sons of God are the chosen line that came out of Seth, who replaced Abel after Cain killed him.

“There were giants in the earth in those days; and also after that, when the sons of God came in unto the daughters of men, and they bare children to them, the same became mighty men which were of old, men of renown.” Then: “God saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually.” The wickedness of verse 5 is that very thing: the sons of God taking the daughters of men to themselves, when the Most High had said not to do it.

“And it repented the Lord that he had made man on the earth, and it grieved him at his heart.” Now we know why the Most High told Abraham that his seed would surely end up serving in Egypt four hundred years. As the sons of God we broke his laws, and he brought forth judgment, rightfully so.

Genesis 6 says “the sons of God saw the daughters of men,” and the question always comes: who are the sons of God, and what line do they come out of? Luke 3:38 answers it at the end of Christ’s genealogy: “Which was the son of Enos, which was the son of Seth, which was the son of Adam, which was the son of God.”

That is the lineage of the sons of God. Adam is called the son of God, and the chosen line runs from him through Seth. Of Adam’s sons, Abel was put to death, and Seth replaced him; the sons of God came out of Seth’s line, down to Enos and on to Noah, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.

Write that down so the next time the question comes up you are not confused. It explains the promise to Abram: “thy seed shall be a stranger in a land that is not theirs.” The sons of God of Seth’s line broke God’s law by mixing with the daughters of men, and the judgment came down on the same chosen line: Jacob’s children went into Egypt and served in hard bondage four hundred years.

Keeping the seventh day holy means more than not going to the job. Exodus 16:23 shows how the food is handled: “To morrow is the rest of the holy sabbath unto the Lord: bake that which ye will bake to day, and seethe that ye will seethe; and that which remaineth over lay up for you to be kept until the morning.”

So before Friday sundown, before complete darkness, you are to lay up your food for the next day, because there is no cooking on the Sabbath. Whatever needs baking or boiling is done the day before, and what is left over is kept for the holy day.

This is one of the laws that apply to the Sabbath, and it follows from Genesis 2:2-3: God “rested on the seventh day from all his work,” and he “blessed the seventh day, and sanctified it.” His people rest the same way, preparing ahead so that the seventh day stays free of labour.

“And on the seventh day God ended his work which he had made; and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had made.” The seventh day is not Sunday. And the number seven represents completion, perfection; hold on to that, because it runs through everything that follows.

For those who are new, the Sabbath has rules. Is coming together to congregate enough? No. There are laws that apply to the Sabbath day, and the first is the commandment itself: “Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy. Six days shalt thou labour, and do all thy work: But the seventh day is the sabbath of the Lord thy God: in it thou shalt not do any work.”

So there is no working, no servile work, on the Sabbath. The commandment reaches the whole house: “thou, nor thy son, nor thy daughter, thy manservant, nor thy maidservant, nor thy cattle, nor thy stranger that is within thy gates.”

The pattern is the one God set in Genesis 2: six days of work, and on the seventh he rested. God “blessed the seventh day, and sanctified it: because that in it he had rested from all his work.” We keep it holy because he made it holy, and our rest from servile work on that day is a similitude of the true rest still to come, when we reign with Christ.

Many brothers coming out of the different religions think the Sabbath is for everyone. Exodus 31 shows who it was given to, and how seriously the Most High takes it: “Ye shall keep the sabbath therefore; for it is holy unto you: every one that defileth it shall surely be put to death: for whosoever doeth any work therein, that soul shall be cut off from among his people.”

It is “holy unto you,” to Israel. And the penalty written for defiling it, death and being cut off from among his people, shows how much weight God puts on it. It is not a day to congregate and then go about our own business; doing any work on it was a matter of life and death.

That weight comes from Genesis 2:3: “God blessed the seventh day, and sanctified it.” What God sanctifies, his people are not to make common.

Who is the Sabbath for? Exodus 31:16-17: “Wherefore the children of Israel shall keep the sabbath, to observe the sabbath throughout their generations, for a perpetual covenant. It is a sign between me and the children of Israel for ever.” Not between God and the Ammonites, not between God and the white man: the children of Israel only. When Christ comes back, yes, everyone will be made to keep the Sabbath; but the Sabbath was created for one people, the Israelites.

The reason given ties it straight to Genesis 2: “for in six days the Lord made heaven and earth, and on the seventh day he rested, and was refreshed.” The same seventh day of Genesis 2:2 is the sign of the covenant.

And it points ahead. Paul writes, “For he spake in a certain place of the seventh day on this wise, And God did rest the seventh day from all his works,” and “There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God.” The rest in the land under Joshua was not the true rest; there were enemies on every side. Resting from servile work on the seventh day is a similitude of the true rest: when Christ comes back and we reign with him a thousand years. That is why seven means completion, perfection.

Another law of the Sabbath: “Ye shall kindle no fire throughout your habitations upon the sabbath day.”

That is not talking about turning on the heat when it is freezing in the house. It is talking about cooking: do not kindle a fire to cook on the Sabbath. It goes together with Exodus 16:23, where the food is baked and boiled the day before and laid up until the morning.

And stop following Amalek, the so-called Jewish people who are not the real Jews, who add to the law with their Talmud, their oral law. Their additions make the Sabbath a burden God never put on it. The commandment is what is written: no cooking fire in our habitations on the day God blessed and sanctified, the seventh day on which he “rested from all his work which God created and made.”

Lamech’s “seventy and sevenfold” was complete vengeance, and Edom carries that same spirit. Amos 1:11: “Thus saith the Lord; For three transgressions of Edom, and for four, I will not turn away the punishment thereof; because he did pursue his brother with the sword, and did cast off all pity, and his anger did tear perpetually, and he kept his wrath for ever.”

He pursued his brother Jacob with the sword. He cast off all pity. His anger tore perpetually, and “he kept his wrath for ever.” Forever, perpetual: he hates our guts, and it does not wear off with time.

That is why we cannot trust this man, and why people wonder to this day why they still treat us the way they do. He has not forgotten how we ruled over him, and he is still acting out his vengeance. The Lord has seen it, and he says he will not turn away the punishment for it.

This is the dark side of seventy times seven. On the one side is the murderer’s total vengeance, kept forever; on the other side, as the class went on to show, is Christ answering Peter, “I say not unto thee, Until seven times: but, Until seventy times seven”: complete, boundless mercy for Israel.

God said of Cain, “whosoever slayeth Cain, vengeance shall be taken on him sevenfold.” Then Cain’s great-great-grandson Lamech boasted to his wives, Adah and Zillah: “I have slain a man to my wounding, and a young man to my hurt. If Cain shall be avenged sevenfold, truly Lamech seventy and sevenfold.” He walked in the same footsteps as Cain; through regeneration it would be no surprise if Lamech were Cain all over again. Seventy and sevenfold in the mouth of a murderer means complete vengeance: total and utter.

That is why Ecclesiasticus says never trust thine enemy. You think he forgot how we handled him under King David, when we put garrisons over him and pushed him off the mountains? Or that we pushed him into the wilderness, where they became the wildlings of the dark ages? He has not forgotten. He is still acting out his vengeance on the so-called blacks and Hispanics to this day.

Ezekiel 35:5 names it: “Because thou hast had a perpetual hatred, and hast shed the blood of the children of Israel by the force of the sword in the time of their calamity, in the time that their iniquity had an end.” Perpetual hatred is great hatred, ongoing hatred, fiery hatred. That is Lamech’s seventy and sevenfold carried on through Edom.

The death of Patrice Lumumba shows it. One of the officers responsible spoke on video, laughing, this damn devil: they chopped up his body and poured acid on it, and he kept Lumumba’s gold tooth. His family held it until it was recently flown back to the Congo. The same was done to Nat Turner, whose skull was passed down as an heirloom, a trophy. These people are the damn devil the Bible speaks of, and that is the perpetual hatred.

Edom’s hatred is perpetual, like Lamech’s vengeance, “seventy and sevenfold,” complete and total. But God has spoken on what will come of it. Obadiah 1:10: “For thy violence against thy brother Jacob shame shall cover thee, and thou shalt be cut off for ever.”

For his violence against his brother Jacob, shame shall cover him, and he shall be cut off forever. His wrath is kept forever, and his end is forever too.

So Lamech’s seventy and seven was complete vengeance, driven by hatred, perpetual hatred. Then comes the flip side. Peter asked, “Lord, how oft shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? till seven times?” and “Jesus saith unto him, I say not unto thee, Until seven times: but, Until seventy times seven.” Christ took the same number and made it complete mercy. He forgave us through all our captivities, and he commands us to forgive our brother the same way, while the enemy who kept his wrath for ever is cut off for ever.

“Purge out therefore the old leaven, that ye may be a new lump, as ye are unleavened. For even Christ our passover is sacrificed for us”.

The old leaven is sin. Purge it out, that you may be a new lump. Because Christ our passover is sacrificed for us.

Christ was that unleavened bread that laid his life down for the children of Israel. So the passover and the feast of unleavened bread in Leviticus 23:5-6 both come to him: he is the lamb and he is the bread. With these the class counted three of the seven so far: the Sabbath, the passover, and the feast of unleavened bread.

Peter shows who that lamb without blemish was: “ye were not redeemed with corruptible things, as silver and gold, from your vain conversation received by tradition from your fathers; But with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot”.

So Christ was that lamb without blemish, the same thing Exodus 12:5 required. Without blemish and without spot. He is the one “foreordained before the foundation of the world, but was manifest in these last times for you”.

That is what John the Baptist said of Christ when he saw him coming: Behold the Lamb of God that takes away the sins of the world. The passover of Leviticus 23:5 is fulfilled in him.

Still in the passover instructions: “In one house shall it be eaten; thou shalt not carry forth ought of the flesh abroad out of the house; neither shall ye break a bone thereof.”

Neither shall ye break a bone thereof. Those are the instructions for how to slaughter the lamb: do not break the bones of it.

That one command is going to be fulfilled to the letter in Christ. The high holy day of passover that we just went over is a picture of him, down to his bones.

Leviticus 23 lays out the feasts of the Lord, seven of them in that chapter, and every single one of them represents Jesus Christ. The first annual one is the Lord’s passover, “In the fourteenth day of the first month at even”, the high holy day we just celebrated. So we go back to the instructions for the passover lamb.

“Your lamb shall be without blemish, a male of the first year: ye shall take it out from the sheep, or from the goats”. Without blemish, a male of the first year. That is the lamb our forefathers had to choose.

That lamb without blemish is the pattern of Christ. The passover is a representation of Christ laying down his life for us, and everything spoken of the lamb in Exodus 12 points to him.

This is the fulfilment. “The Jews therefore, because it was the preparation, that the bodies should not remain upon the cross on the sabbath day, (for that sabbath day was an high day,) besought Pilate that their legs might be broken”.

“Then came the soldiers, and brake the legs of the first, and of the other which was crucified with him. But when they came to Jesus, and saw that he was dead already, they brake not his legs”.

They broke the legs of the two crucified with him, but not his. Thus fulfilling the prophecy in Psalms 34:20, and the passover command, neither shall ye break a bone thereof. Christ was that passover lamb, and there is still more meat to scrape off the bones of this.

After passover comes the next feast: “on the fifteenth day of the same month is the feast of unleavened bread unto the Lord: seven days ye must eat unleavened bread.” There is that seven again.

The unleavened bread represents Christ: his sinless life, not having leaven. We know the history too, the Most High wanted us to hurry up and leave Egypt, so there was no time to sit and bake bread. But it also goes into Christ’s unleavened life, sinless and blameless.

Christ says it: “I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger”. He is the bread of life, the unleavened bread of the feast.

“And Joseph also went up from Galilee, out of the city of Nazareth, into Judea, unto the city of David, which is called Bethlehem; (because he was of the house and lineage of David:) To be taxed with Mary his espoused wife, being great with child.”

To be taxed together you have to be married, brothers. You have to have papers, jointly. Not a toilet paper: years ago a brother wrote an instrument of divorce on toilet paper, because he did not really value her or count her as his wife.

“And so it was, that, while they were there, the days were accomplished that she should be delivered. And she brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes”. They wrapped Christ in swaddling clothes, the same thing our forefathers did with the lambs when they brought them to Jerusalem.

Born in Bethlehem where the passover lambs were raised, wrapped the way they were wrapped, offered in Jerusalem at passover. Thus fulfilling prophecy. So we know Christ was our passover.

The lambs without blemish were raised in Bethlehem and slaughtered in Jerusalem. Same thing as Jesus Christ. So the prophecy: “But thou, Beth–lehem Ephratah, though thou be little among the thousands of Judah, yet out of thee shall he come forth unto me that is to be ruler in Israel; whose goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting.”

Christ was born in Bethlehem. An article read in the class shows how our forefathers handled the passover lambs: the high priests given charge over them brought forth lambs without blemish from Migdal Eder in Bethlehem, wrapped in cloths, and brought them to Jerusalem for sacrifice. Migdal Eder means the tower of the flock, the same tower of the flock read about in Micah the fourth chapter, the eighth verse.

This Jesus was born in Bethlehem, wrapped in cloths, and eventually brought to Jerusalem during passover, where he offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins. The same road as the lambs.

Here is the prophecy about Christ: “He keepeth all his bones: not one of them is broken.”

What was commanded for the passover lamb in Exodus 12:46, “neither shall ye break a bone thereof”, is written here as a prophecy of the Messiah. Not one of his bones would be broken.

The passover is a representation of Christ laying down his life for us, and the Psalms spoke it ahead of time, so that when it came to pass we would know he is our passover.

The two wave loaves are “the firstfruits unto the Lord”, and Christ is “the firstfruits of them that slept”. He rose first, and the same promise stands for all who believe and keep the commandments in the faith of Christ.
God begat us “with the word of truth, that we should be a kind of firstfruits of his creatures.” Following Christ's example, his people become the offering the feast of firstfruits pictured.

The firstfruits are those who “follow the Lamb whithersoever he goeth”, kept clean from false doctrine and philosophy as well as literal defilement. They are “the firstfruits unto God and to the Lamb.”

The feast offers “the firstfruits unto the Lord”, and those who repent in Christ are meant to be firstfruits too, the best of the best. We carry “the firstfruits of the Spirit” while we wait for “the redemption of our body”.
The trumpet of this feast is no soft flute. When it sounds, every man shall “be suddenly afraid”, a frightening call that tells of Christ's coming.

The feast of trumpets points to Christ, who “shall send his angels with a great sound of a trumpet” to gather his elect. That elect is Israel, the people scattered “from one end of heaven to the other.”
When “the Lord God shall blow the trumpet”, he rises to defend his people and save them “as the flock of his people”. The memorial of trumpets looks ahead to that day of rescue for Israel.
Christ “is the propitiation for our sins”, the atonement this day pointed to. The “whole world” here is scattered Israel, all Israel, given time to repent.

Christ was that atonement. The old priests died and had to be replaced, but he “continueth ever” and “ever liveth to make intercession”, so with no death in him he can atone for his people continually.

The day of atonement needed blood, and Christ entered the holy place “by his own blood”, once, “having obtained eternal redemption for us.” A testament takes force only after the testator dies, so Christ had to die.
Propitiation means atonement. God set Christ forth “to be a propitiation through faith in his blood”, so he is the true day of atonement, “for the remission of sins that are past”.
On Aaron's long garment a stone stood for each tribe, so “in the long garment was the whole world”, meaning Israel. Christ is now the new high priest who makes atonement for that people.
Tabernacle, sukkot, booth: it means to dwell. When “the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us”, Christ pitched his tent among his people, the true feast of tabernacles.
Christ said “Destroy this temple”, but “he spake of the temple of his body.” His body was the greater and more perfect tabernacle, not made with hands, where God dwelt among us.
Tabernacle means to dwell, and here “the tabernacle of God is with men, and he will dwell with them.” He is the God of Israel, and this is the completion every feast was pointing to.

Numbers 14:22 says they “have tempted me now these ten times, and have not hearkened to my voice”. These ten times are the countless acts of stubbornness of the children of Israel, and that is why the Lord asked “How long will this people provoke me?” Write them down. The Most High deals in numbers, and nothing in the Bible is insignificant.

Number one is at the Red Sea. “And they said unto Moses, Because there were no graves in Egypt, hast thou taken us away to die in the wilderness? wherefore hast thou dealt thus with us, to carry us forth out of Egypt? Is not this the word that we did tell thee in Egypt, saying, Let us alone, that we may serve the Egyptians? For it had been better for us to serve the Egyptians, than that we should die in the wilderness.”

They were complaining to Moses. The Lord had just brought them out with his glory and his miracles, and the first thing they did at the sea was wish themselves back in Egypt serving the Egyptians.

Number two of the ten times the children of Israel tempted the Lord is at Marah, m-a-r-a-h. Write it down so you are not confused if it comes up again.

“And when they came to Marah, they could not drink of the waters of Marah, for they were bitter: therefore the name of it was called Marah. And the people murmured against Moses, saying, What shall we drink?”

The people complained because the water was bitter. They had just seen the Lord overthrow the Egyptians in the midst of the sea, and at the first bitter water they murmured against Moses. That is the provoking the Lord speaks of in Numbers 14:22: men “which have seen my glory, and my miracles”, and still did not hearken to his voice.

Number four is the hoarding of the manna. “And Moses said, Let no man leave of it till the morning.” Moses gave specific instructions: do not leave any of the manna until the morning.

“Notwithstanding they hearkened not unto Moses; but some of them left of it until the morning, and it bred worms, and stank: and Moses was wroth with them.” Moses just told you. And they said, the hell with you; we want to replace you anyway. That is the mindset of our people.

This is what the Lord means in Numbers 14:22 when he says they “have not hearkened to my voice.” He fed them bread from heaven, gave one plain instruction, and they would not keep it.

Number three is the wilderness of Sin. “And the whole congregation of the children of Israel murmured against Moses and Aaron in the wilderness”. Do you notice a trend here?

“Would to God we had died by the hand of the Lord in the land of Egypt, when we sat by the flesh pots, and when we did eat bread to the full; for ye have brought us forth into this wilderness, to kill this whole assembly with hunger.”

It is going to be the same thing when Christ comes back, but Christ is not playing games with us this time; he did not play games back then either. This time it will be ten times worse, ten times more severe, ten times more strict. When we are saved out of this modern day Egypt, Babylon the Great, America, the United Snakes of America, and Christ brings us into the wilderness, that grace is finished. No more I should have, could have, would have, I made a mistake. That is over with.

Number five is the Sabbath manna. “And it came to pass, that there went out some of the people on the seventh day for to gather, and they found none. And the Lord said unto Moses, How long refuse ye to keep my commandments and my laws? See, for that the Lord hath given you the sabbath, therefore he giveth you on the sixth day the bread of two days; abide ye every man in his place, let no man go out of his place on the seventh day.”

They were supposed to gather extra on the sixth day; the Most High gave them enough manna to lay up for two days. And they said, no, Lord, we are going out on the seventh day to get this manna. Forgetting everything the Most High did for us in bringing us up out of Egypt. No gratitude. We are a people of no gratitude at all.

Number six is at Massah and Meribah. “Wherefore the people did chide with Moses, and said, Give us water that we may drink.” To chide means to murmur, to be contentious, to go back and forth. “And Moses said unto them, Why chide ye with me? wherefore do ye tempt the Lord?”

Then, “the people murmured against Moses, and said, Wherefore is this that thou hast brought us up out of Egypt, to kill us and our children and our cattle with thirst? And Moses cried unto the Lord, saying, What shall I do unto this people? they be almost ready to stone me.” They were almost ready to stone the man who brought them out of Egypt, over water.

The Lord said, “Behold, I will stand before thee there upon the rock in Horeb; and thou shalt smite the rock, and there shall come water out of it, that the people may drink.” And Moses “called the name of the place Massah, and Meribah, because of the chiding of the children of Israel, and because they tempted the Lord, saying, Is the Lord among us, or not?”

That is the very word Numbers 14:22 uses: they have “tempted me now these ten times.” The place itself was named for it.

Number seven is the golden calf. “And when the people saw that Moses delayed to come down out of the mount, the people gathered themselves together unto Aaron, and said unto him, Up, make us gods, which shall go before us; for as for this Moses, the man that brought us up out of the land of Egypt, we wot not what is become of him.”

That is the no gratitude. The Most High just showed all those wonderful plagues and destroyed your enemy, and now you want a different god, a god of silver, gold and wood, a god that cannot talk. And look how disrespectful: as for this Moses. No different from our people who despise this truth and want to go back to Christianity, who prefer white Jesus, or who run to the east, to Mecca, and pray to a damn cobblestone that cannot talk back or answer prayers. That is why the Most High says we are dumber than an ox.

Aaron, the high priest, got real simple here, but it was out of fear, and he knew better. Then, “he received them at their hand, and fashioned it with a graving tool, after he had made it a molten calf”; he had the skills of a blacksmith and turned the gold they spoiled from Egypt into idolatry. It was the people who said “These be thy gods, O Israel, which brought thee up out of the land of Egypt.” Then “the people sat down to eat and to drink, and rose up to play”: in honour of that pagan god they had orgies.

“They have turned aside quickly out of the way which I commanded them”. “I have seen this people, and, behold, it is a stiffnecked people: Now therefore let me alone, that my wrath may wax hot against them, and that I may consume them”. Yes, we are a stiffnecked people, and only Moses standing in the gap turned it away, as he did again in Numbers 14.

Number eight is Taberah. “And when the people complained, it displeased the Lord: and the Lord heard it; and his anger was kindled; and the fire of the Lord burnt among them, and consumed them that were in the uttermost parts of the camp.” More complaining, and the Most High started burning people with fire, the same thing he is going to do in America. “And the people cried unto Moses; and when Moses prayed unto the Lord, the fire was quenched.”

Then the lusting for flesh: “the mixt multitude that was among them fell a lusting: and the children of Israel also wept again, and said, Who shall give us flesh to eat? We remember the fish, which we did eat in Egypt freely; the cucumbers, and the melons, and the leeks, and the onions, and the garlick”. Always about food; black people for you.

“But now our soul is dried away: there is nothing at all, beside this manna, before our eyes.” Ungrateful, complaining about the manna. Over and over the Lord was longsuffering, and over and over Moses prayed and the Lord pardoned, as Numbers 14:20 says: “I have pardoned according to thy word”.

Number nine: the lusting for flesh ended in a graveyard. “And he called the name of that place Kibroth–hattaavah: because there they buried the people that lusted.” Taberah was number eight; Kibroth-hattaavah is number nine.

Number ten is the report of the spies, the doubt and fear of Numbers 13 and 14, and there the Most High had enough. “Surely they shall not see the land which I sware unto their fathers, neither shall any of them that provoked me see it”. Everyone twenty and upward fell in the wilderness, save Caleb and Joshua.

The Most High deals in numbers, and everything in the Bible is significant. Ten times he was longsuffering, and places like Kibroth-hattaavah still carry the names of what our fathers did.

“the Lord was with Joseph, and he was a prosperous man.” His master saw that the Lord was with him and made him overseer over his house, and “the Lord blessed the Egyptian’s house for Joseph’s sake.” And “Joseph was a goodly person, and well favoured”: he had a very good reputation, and people looked at him as a man of integrity and good character.

blog/2026/2026-05-26-2026-05-26-the-supe:
In Exodus 1 the new king says “the people of the children of Israel are more and mightier than we: Come on, let us deal wisely with them.” The Egyptians were tall and strong, yet they said the Hebrews were mightier; something had happened for them to know it. They could not destroy us head on, so they set up institutions of oppression to keep us beneath them. There is nothing new under the sun, and Jim Crow was already around in Joseph’s time.

Genesis 43:32: “And they set on for him by himself, and for them by themselves, and for the Egyptians, which did eat with him, by themselves: because the Egyptians might not eat bread with the Hebrews; for that is an abomination unto the Egyptians.”

Joseph had status. He was second over Egypt, the governor, the vizier, and still he was not granted the privileges of a full-blooded Egyptian. His Egyptian servants could not sit with him; they had their own table and he had his. He was a resource they could use, because his God gave him the dreams that kept them from famine, but he could not sit at their table because he was a Hebrew. It was an abomination for an Egyptian to eat with a Hebrew.

That is Jim Crow: Egyptians sit here, Hebrews sit there; whites sit here, coloreds sit there. The same people who used Joseph’s wisdom kept him apart, and the same thinking later dealt wisely with us in Egypt and in America.

Did it change after Joseph’s table? No. When his family came down, Joseph told them what to say to Pharaoh. “the men are shepherds, for their trade hath been to feed cattle;” and when Pharaoh asks, “What is your occupation?” they were to answer: “Thy servants’ trade hath been about cattle from our youth even until now, both we, and also our fathers: that ye may dwell in the land of Goshen; for every shepherd is an abomination unto the Egyptians.”

The Israelites were known as shepherds. Because of the war with the shepherd kings before Joseph arrived, the Egyptians hated shepherds, so the Israelites were despised twice over, as Hebrews and as shepherds.

So Israel was placed in Goshen, an isolated area away from the Egyptians. Egyptians and shepherds could not live in the same vicinity, which means there were no Egyptians living among us to put their blood into ours. That is segregation; that is redlining. It is nothing new.

That separation is the ground Exodus 1 grows out of. A people set apart, more and mightier than their masters, “dealt wisely” with: taskmasters over them, building Pithom and Raamses, serving “with rigour” in mortar, brick and “all manner of service in the field.” The same pattern followed us into America: set apart, built the Capitol and the White House, worked the fields.

The Lord called Bezaleel the son of Uri of the tribe of Judah and filled him “with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship”. A goldsmith, a silversmith, a brass worker, a stone cutter, a wood carver: one man. And with him Aholiab of the tribe of Dan, a partner.

Here is the work being done: “Then wrought Bezaleel and Aholiab, and every wise hearted man, in whom the Lord put wisdom and understanding to know how to work all manner of work for the service of the sanctuary, according to all that the Lord had commanded.”

Those two were the main men, and they had a team under them to create these things. “And Moses called Bezaleel and Aholiab, and every wise hearted man, in whose heart the Lord had put wisdom, even every one whose heart stirred him up to come unto the work to do it”.

We read of the tabernacle, the ark, the mercy seat, the furniture, the candlestick, the altars, the laver, the clothes of service, the holy garments tailored for Aaron, the anointing oil and the incense, and never realize who was behind making them. They did not fall out of the sky. Somebody made every one of them: our forefathers, filled with the wisdom of the Most High. Exodus 37:1-29 gives exactly what they made, in detail.

That is the superiority of the chosen people. The Bible means what it says: these were geniuses, and they were Israel.

“And Jacob was left alone; and there wrestled a man with him until the breaking of the day.” He fought for hours. In a real fight you are exhausted long before daybreak; a boxing match is twelve rounds, and Jacob fought until the break of day. “when he saw that he prevailed not against him, he touched the hollow of his thigh;” and put it out of joint. The angel had to dislocate Jacob’s thigh to stop him. Even then Jacob held on: “I will not let thee go, except thou bless me.”

“Thy name shall be called no more Jacob, but Israel: for as a prince hast thou power with God and with men, and hast prevailed.” That is what the name means: a prince with power with God.

Hosea 12:3-4 says why his name was changed: “He took his brother by the heel in the womb, and by his strength he had power with God: Yea, he had power over the angel, and prevailed: he wept, and made supplication unto him: he found him in Beth–el, and there he spake with us.” By his strength. His name was changed to Israel because of how strong he was. This was no slap boxing; it went back and forth, and there is no other record in the Bible of any man wrestling with an angel and prevailing. Jacob was a god on the earth.

He was trained to fight. Abraham had trained servants, armed them, and went to war to bring Lot back; Isaac knew it as well, and they taught Jacob. Imagine his descendants: David running through warriors, Samson, a warlike race. Our forefathers were intellectual as well as physically powerful; Abraham knew arithmetic and taught astronomy. That is why this superiority is stressed: white people, and even some of our own who move in their circles, say we are stupid and have low IQ, and many of us believe it. The white teacher told Malcolm X, top of his class, that being a lawyer was no profession for a nigga, and he should be a carpenter. The scriptures say otherwise about the children of Israel.

“Judah is a lion’s whelp.” He was a young lion in the 1960s, and after that he fell and became the old lion: “who shall rouse him up?” Then: “The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor a lawgiver from between his feet, until Shiloh come; and unto him shall the gathering of the people be.” Shiloh is Christ, and unto him, and to Judah, shall the gathering of the people be. Judah is the essential tribe to bring all twelve tribes together, the very liberation the 1969 hearings feared, which is why they said they had to destroy Judah among the African American community: education, revised Bibles, contraception, autism, using all they can to destroy these negroes.

Deuteronomy 33:7 is Moses’ blessing on the same tribe: “And this is the blessing of Judah: and he said, Hear, Lord, the voice of Judah, and bring him unto his people: let his hands be sufficient for him; and be thou an help to him from his enemies.” Bring Judah unto his people on an international scale: bring Judah to all the tribes, so that we can get out of here. Judah, Benjamin and Levi are giving these devils hell, and all twelve tribes are going to rise up together and bring hell to this kingdom.

It is already happening. A sister in Papua New Guinea wrote to one of our groups that her people thought they were free of colonization after independence in 1975, but religion still holds them colonized, enslaved, trapped and in poverty. Her answer was to go back to the origins of the Bible, obey it, and see what the Lord can do for their country: Genesis 49:8-12, and to listen to the tribe of Judah, who holds the sceptre, whom all tribes shall praise. Our people there know Judah has been sent to revive them.

That is why Judah in America is kept down. Every other tribe, in Jamaica, in Africa, in Europe, Levi speaking six languages, is better educated than Judah here. If Judah knew five or six languages, this thing would be over quickly. So the schools are dumbed down for Judah, while the blessing stands: the Lord will hear Judah’s voice, bring him to his people, and help him against his enemies.

“God standeth in the congregation of the mighty; he judgeth among the gods.” Who are the gods he judges among? The law answers it: “Thou shalt not revile the gods, nor curse the ruler of thy people.”

The gods and the ruler of thy people are the same men. The gods are our leaders, our judges. God always moved through the leadership of our forefathers: through Moses, through Aaron, through the captains and the officers. The spirit of the Lord would move and judge us through the leaders that were acting and moving correctly in that time.

So when the psalm says he judgeth among the gods, it is referring to our leaders, the men of Israel. That is why the psalm can go on to say “all the foundations of the earth are out of course”: when our leadership walked on in darkness and Israel went into sin, the world went out of order, because its rightful heirs and rulers are not in their proper place.

And that is why the Lord could say “Ye are gods; and all of you are children of the most High.” It was not a term of endearment; he meant it. The men of the children of Israel are gods, and because of that we cannot afford low self-esteem or an inferiority complex.
blog/2026/2026-05-30-2026-05-30-joseph-i:
When Joseph’s brothers sat down to eat bread, they saw “a company of Ishmeelites came from Gilead with their camels bearing spicery and balm and myrrh, going to carry it down to Egypt.” Judah said, “What profit is it if we slay our brother, and conceal his blood? Come, and let us sell him to the Ishmeelites.” Then the verse changes names: “Then there passed by Midianites merchantmen; and they drew and lifted up Joseph out of the pit, and sold Joseph to the Ishmeelites for twenty pieces of silver.”

There are always questions about the Midianites and the Ishmaelites. Genesis 25 shows who the Midianites were: “Then again Abraham took a wife, and her name was Keturah. And she bare him Zimran, and Jokshan, and Medan, and Midian, and Ishbak, and Shuah.” Keturah had six sons by Abraham, and Midian is one of them. The chapter goes on to his sons: “And the sons of Midian; Ephah, and Epher, and Hanoch, and Abida, and Eldaah. All these were the children of Keturah.”

So the Midianites are Abraham’s children through Keturah, just as the Ishmaelites are Abraham’s children through Hagar. They were working together and roaming the land together, all Abraham’s kids, and they looked very similar. That is why the story says Ishmaelites, then Midianites, then “the Midianites sold him into Egypt unto Potiphar,” and then in Genesis 39 Potiphar “bought him of the hands of the Ishmeelites.” It is not a contradiction; these groups were together.

Genesis 37 names both groups in the sale of Joseph: the Midianites drew him out of the pit and “sold Joseph to the Ishmeelites for twenty pieces of silver,” and later “the Midianites sold him into Egypt unto Potiphar.” Genesis 25:12 shows who the Ishmaelites were: “Now these are the generations of Ishmael, Abraham’s son, whom Hagar the Egyptian, Sarah’s handmaid, bare unto Abraham.”

Abraham had Ishmael from Hagar, and Ishmael had sons as well: Nebajoth the firstborn, “and Kedar, and Adbeel, and Mibsam, And Mishma, and Dumah, and Massa, Hadar, and Tema, Jetur, Naphish, and Kedemah.” “These are the sons of Ishmael, and these are their names, by their towns, and by their castles; twelve princes according to their nations.”

Abraham’s children from Keturah and Abraham’s children from Hagar always lived together and worked together. So when a company of Ishmaelites comes by carrying spices down to Egypt and Midianite merchantmen are among them, it is one caravan of Abraham’s other children traveling side by side.

Meanwhile the brothers, so envious of Joseph, dipped his coat of many colours in the blood of a kid of the goats and let Jacob believe “an evil beast hath devoured him.” Reuben had suggested the pit so he could come back and save him, and when he returned, “Joseph was not in the pit; and he rent his clothes.” Envy will have you do evil things. Remember Reuben’s character; it plays a part later.

Joseph was seventeen, a teenager, sold into Egypt: “Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh, captain of the guard, an Egyptian, bought him of the hands of the Ishmeelites.” Yet “the Lord was with Joseph, and he was a prosperous man.” His master “saw that the Lord was with him, and that the Lord made all that he did to prosper in his hand,” and made him overseer over his house, putting all that he had into his hand.

Luke 16:10 explains why: “He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much: and he that is unjust in the least is unjust also in much.” Joseph was in slavery, but he was faithful to Potiphar, and Potiphar raised him up.

It speaks to us today. Many brothers and sisters have jobs, and the Most High is observing us in whatever we do. The least that we are faithful in is these little jobs out here. Just as Joseph was in captivity, we are in captivity, but that does not mean we can steal, lie or rob. When you are on your jobs, do not steal; deal right. God is watching each and every one of us.

And look what faithfulness brought: “the Lord blessed the Egyptian’s house for Joseph’s sake; and the blessing of the Lord was upon all that he had in the house, and in the field.” The theme is the same as when Jacob worked for Laban all those years and Laban was blessed for Jacob’s sake. Faithful in little, Joseph was trusted with much, until his master “knew not ought he had, save the bread which he did eat.”

When Potiphar’s wife could not get her way, she lied. She called the men of her house and said, “See, he hath brought in an Hebrew unto us to mock us; he came in unto me to lie with me, and I cried with a loud voice.” Then “she laid up his garment by her, until his lord came home”: she kept his clothes as false evidence, and told her husband the same lie.

Sirach shows what that kind of tongue does: “A backbiting tongue hath disquieted many, and driven them from nation to nation: strong cities hath it pulled down, and overthrown the houses of great men.” Somebody that lies on you can do much destruction. Joseph was the greatest man in Potiphar's house, trusted with everything, and a lying tongue brought him down to the king's prison.

It is the same today. Many brothers have been locked up because a woman lied on them: an ex-wife or ex-girlfriend who wants his life to go down the tubes, who calls him over, is refused, and then threatens to tell the police he hurt her. Others are in jail because a woman started a fight and expected him to defend her. Don't deal with a woman like that; that is the kind of woman Joseph had over him.

And this same spirit met our people in slavery. A lot of us were put to death because of it. Emmett Till was put to death for the lying woman, and there are a lot of cases like that. What Potiphar's wife did to Joseph, a backbiting tongue has done to Israel again and again.

Sirach goes on: “Many have fallen by the edge of the sword: but not so many as have fallen by the tongue.” The tongue does a lot of evil, and that is exactly what Potiphar’s wife did to Joseph. She never lifted a sword against him; she only spoke, and her words did the work.

She told her husband, “The Hebrew servant, which thou hast brought unto us, came in unto me to mock me,” and “when his master heard the words of his wife,” “his wrath was kindled.” On nothing but her word, “Joseph’s master took him, and put him into the prison, a place where the king’s prisoners were bound.” Remember how old Joseph is here: 17.

That is how our people have fallen too: brothers in prison on a lie, and in slavery times men like Emmett Till put to death because of a lying woman's words. More have fallen by the tongue than by the sword. Guard yourself from the kind of company that can destroy you with a word.

Joseph was 17, falsely accused, and thrown into the king's prison. Sirach tells you why this should not shock a servant of God: “My son, if thou come to serve the Lord, prepare thy soul for temptation.” Joseph understood this, because his father Jacob taught him.

“Set thy heart aright, and constantly endure, and make not haste in time of trouble.” Make not haste means don't leave this truth in your time of trouble. Satan will tell you, if you weren't in that Bible you wouldn't be going through half of what you're going through; you had it better when you served me. “Cleave unto him, and depart not away, that thou mayest be increased at thy last end.”

“Whatsoever is brought upon thee take cheerfully, and be patient when thou art changed to a low estate.” Joseph's family was rich; Jacob was a wealthy man. Joseph was taken from all that, sold as a slave, and now he is in the midst of poverty, in prison, for a crime he refused to commit. That is a low estate, and he bore it without leaving God.

Just as it goes for us, it went for our father Joseph. Israel today has been brought down to a low estate, and the tests and trials come because we serve the Lord. Endure them, cleave unto him, and you will be increased at your last end, as Joseph was.

Even in prison, “the Lord was with Joseph, and shewed him mercy, and gave him favour in the sight of the keeper of the prison.” The keeper “committed to Joseph’s hand all the prisoners that were in the prison,” and “looked not to any thing that was under his hand; because the Lord was with him, and that which he did, the Lord made it to prosper.”

Solomon gives the reason: “When a man’s ways please the Lord, he maketh even his enemies to be at peace with him.” That is what happened with Joseph. He was a Hebrew slave, accused of attacking his master's wife, locked in the place where the king's prisoners were bound, and his very jailer became favourable to him and handed him the whole prison.

It is the same pattern all through Joseph's life: in Potiphar's house the Lord blessed the Egyptian's house “for Joseph’s sake,” just as Laban was blessed for Jacob's sake when Jacob worked for him. Joseph's ways pleased the Lord; he refused sin even when it cost him, and whatever he did, the Lord made it to prosper. Keep your ways pleasing to God, and he will make even those set over you in captivity to be at peace with you.

Potiphar’s wife cast her eyes upon Joseph and said, “Lie with me.” Joseph refused, and he did not refuse half-heartedly: “how then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?” Notice he was not blaming God that he was a slave in a strange land. His master had kept nothing back from him “but thee, because thou art his wife,” and Joseph would not touch her.

This was not a single moment. “she spake to Joseph day by day”; she was trying to wear him down day by day. And the Egyptians loved beautiful women; remember when Abraham went down into Egypt, Sarah was in danger because of her beauty. Potiphar’s wife was no ugly woman; she was good on the eyes, and Joseph, at 17 years old, still said no. When she finally “caught him by his garment,” “he left his garment in her hand, and fled, and got him out.”

Sirach gives the precept for what Joseph did: “Flee from sin as from the face of a serpent: for if thou comest too near it, it will bite thee: the teeth thereof are as the teeth of a lion, slaying the souls of men.” Joseph saw sin like a snake, and he ran like a rabbit. If a snake fell into the room right now, everybody would be out of there. That snake is your sin. “All iniquity is as a two edged sword, the wounds whereof cannot be healed.”

Everybody's demon is not the same. For some it is food; for most of the brothers it is sexual demons, and those demons will get you. Put yourself in Joseph's place and be honest about it: many have been put out for adultery two and three times. Take a page out of what our forefather Joseph did: don't stand there and reason with it, don't come near it. Flee.

The butler and the baker of the king of Egypt offended their lord and were put in ward “the place where Joseph was bound.” “they dreamed a dream both of them, each man his dream in one night,” and in the morning they were sad, because “there is no interpreter of it.” Joseph answered, “Do not interpretations belong to God? tell me them, I pray you.”

Sirach speaks to dreams: “The hopes of a man void of understanding are vain and false: and dreams lift up fools.” “Whoso regardeth dreams is like him that catcheth at a shadow, and followeth after the wind.” Don't chase dreams; a man who lives by every dream is grasping at shadows.

But verse 3 gives a clue to understanding the dreams that come from God: “The vision of dreams is the resemblance of one thing to another, even as the likeness of a face to a face.” You may dream about somebody you know, say a man named Joe, and see Joe's face; but it is not Joe. It is someone similar to Joe, maybe in age or in what they do for a living. It could be Bob. You just have to know the people in your circle.

That is how the dreams in Genesis 40 work. The butler's vine with “three branches” and the baker's “three white baskets” were resemblances of one thing to another: the three branches and the three baskets were three days. The interpretation belonged to God, and Joseph gave it.

Jeremiah says the same thing Job said: “Cursed be the day wherein I was born: let not the day wherein my mother bare me be blessed.” Two prophets, and neither one blessed the day of his birth. Put that together with Pharaoh's birthday in Genesis 40, where the baker was hanged at the feast.

We never celebrated birthdays. They are days of narcissism, days to put ourselves up above God. The custom came from the nations; it came through the white man, who got it from what they dug up in their archaeological digs, and then taught that we should be celebrating birthdays.

So stop celebrating that foolishness, even with the excuse that it's for the children. Shut up, you narcissist. It is not of God. It's of the devil. And after that birthday feast, “Yet did not the chief butler remember Joseph, but forgat him.”

Joseph's interpretations came to pass “the third day, which was Pharaoh’s birthday, that he made a feast unto all his servants.” On that birthday “he restored the chief butler unto his butlership again,” “But he hanged the chief baker: as Joseph had interpreted to them.”

Wherever you read of a birthday in scripture, Pharaoh's birthday, Herod's birthday, the birthday of one of the Greek kings, something bad happens. Here a man is hanged at a birthday feast. A birthday is a day of narcissism, a day of proclaiming yourself to be God.

Job shows how the Hebrews felt about the day of their birth: “Let the day perish wherein I was born, and the night in which it was said, There is a man child conceived.” A righteous man did not exalt the day he was born; he wished it would perish. That is why we never celebrated birthdays.

After interpreting the butler's dream, Joseph asked him, “think on me when it shall be well with thee,” and “make mention of me unto Pharaoh, and bring me out of this house:” “For indeed I was stolen away out of the land of the Hebrews: and here also have I done nothing that they should put me into the dungeon.” He wanted out of that dungeon.

Notice the prison is called a dungeon. Lamentations uses the same word: “They have cut off my life in the dungeon, and cast a stone upon me.” To cast a stone upon him means he would never get out. It is speaking of Israel in captivity.

That goes with our political prisoners, who have been in there for a long time, cut off in the dungeon with a stone cast over them. Joseph, stolen away and imprisoned though he had done nothing, is a picture of his people in captivity.

“at the end of two full years” Pharaoh dreamed of seven fat kine eaten up by seven lean kine, and seven good ears devoured by seven thin ears “blasted with the east wind.” None of the magicians could interpret it, until the chief butler remembered his faults and told Pharaoh of the young Hebrew. “Then Pharaoh sent and called Joseph, and they brought him hastily out of the dungeon: and he shaved himself, and changed his raiment, and came in unto Pharaoh.”

Solomon wrote the precept: “Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings; he shall not stand before mean men.” The business is God's business. Joseph was diligent in it in Potiphar's house and in the prison, and now a slave out of the dungeon stands before the king of Egypt. Even there he gave God the glory: “It is not in me: God shall give Pharaoh an answer of peace.”

And he did not come to Pharaoh with only a problem. He told him the dream is one, seven years of plenty and seven of famine, “because the thing is established by God,” and then he told him exactly what to do: appoint officers, take up the fifth part in the plenteous years, and lay up corn against the famine. To every problem, brothers, we must have a solution. Some spirits among us have a problem for every solution; stay away from brothers and sisters like that.

So Pharaoh said, “Can we find such a one as this is, a man in whom the Spirit of God is?” He put his ring upon Joseph's hand, arrayed him in fine linen, made him ride in the second chariot, “and they cried before him, Bow the knee.” We are going to tell the nations that too: bow the knee. “Joseph was thirty years old when he stood before Pharaoh”; he went in at 17 and spent 13 years in servitude and prison before he stood before the king.

This is why you see Israel today meeting dignitaries across the world: because we have been diligent in God's business. Mean men are obscure men, bums on the internet with a handful of followers who want to debate you for clout, whose numbers go up as soon as they see the shirt. They are not worth your time. A man diligent in God's business stands before kings.

Proverbs says “Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings,” and Paul shows which business that is: “Not slothful in business; fervent in spirit; serving the Lord.” That is the proof. The business is God's business, serving the Lord, and you must not be slothful when it comes to it.

“As for Ephraim, their glory shall fly away like a bird, from the birth, and from the womb, and from the conception.” “Though they bring up their children, yet will I bereave them.”

“Ephraim, as I saw Tyrus, is planted in a pleasant place”: that pleasant place is what Moses and Jacob spoke of, the islands, the fruitful bough by a well. “but Ephraim shall bring forth his children to the murderer.” Ephraim would willingly give their children over to improve the race, as the doctrine of la raza taught: wanting children with straight hair, light skin and lighter eyes, not the nappy hair.
